ai.text:
This proposal is a Directive from the European Parliament and Council that aims to simplify and move to digital formats the rules that apply to businesses selling products across the EU's Single Market. It is part of a wider European Commission package to cut paperwork and make it easier for companies to operate and grow, while keeping protections for consumers and the environment. The European Parliament will decide on it under the ordinary legislative procedure, on an equal footing with the Council.

The Commission notes that reporting requirements matter for enforcement and monitoring, and that their costs are largely outweighed by their benefits. However, these requirements can place a disproportionate burden on businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises and micro-companies. Over time they can build up into obligations that are repeated, outdated, poorly timed, or collected in inefficient ways. The Commission's "digital by default" principle aims to address this by making policies digital, interoperable, and adaptable from the start. The proposal is intended to speed up the shift to digital and remove cumbersome paper-based requirements in product law, so companies can submit and share information more easily and national authorities can check compliance more efficiently.

The proposal makes limited, targeted changes to fourteen existing EU product directives covering areas such as noise from outdoor equipment, hazardous substances in electrical goods, recreational craft, pressure equipment, electromagnetic compatibility, measuring instruments, lifts, equipment for explosive atmospheres, radio equipment, and marine equipment. These directives use harmonised standards and a presumption of conformity.

Key changes include requiring the EU declaration of conformity, or similar document, to be drawn up electronically and accessible through an internet address or machine-readable code when it must accompany a product. Manufacturers would also need to show a "digital contact" on products to make it easier for businesses and national authorities to communicate, and once available, the European Business Wallet's digital address could serve this purpose. Product instructions could be provided electronically, except for safety information, which must remain on paper or be marked on the product for consumers. Reporting obligations to national authorities that currently allow "paper or electronic format" would be changed to electronic form only, and exchanges between businesses and competent authorities would be required to happen electronically. The proposal also introduces common specifications as an alternative to harmonised standards, and requires information from the declaration of conformity and instructions to be provided through a digital product passport where other EU law requires one.
